title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: If a cell is 0, zero its entire row and column — in place, with O(1) extra space, by using the first row and column as flag arrays.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given an m×n matrix; if any cell is 0, I need to zero out its entire row and column. In place. And the bonus version asks for O(1) extra space — not O(m + n)."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• In place means mutate the input — no return value, just side effect, right?
• Space target — O(m + n) with separate flag arrays is easy; the interesting version is O(1) extra. Which are you asking for?
• Are zeros that *result* from the wipe themselves triggers? (Important: no — only the *original* zeros trigger.)
• Can m or n be 0?
sections.why: The 'result zeros don't trigger' question is the load-bearing clarification. A naive 'scan, find a zero, wipe row + col' loop will cascade: the zeros it writes become triggers on the next scan, and you wipe the whole matrix. Confirming that only the originals trigger forces a two-pass design (mark, then act) — which is the door to the O(1) solution. The space-target question signals you noticed there's a tiered version of the problem; interviewers often start with O(m + n) and push to O(1).

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(m + n)-space solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: allocate two boolean arrays — `rows` of length m and `cols` of length n. First pass: scan the matrix, and whenever `matrix[i][j] === 0`, set `rows[i] = true` and `cols[j] = true`. Second pass: walk every cell; if `rows[i] || cols[j]`, write 0. O(m*n) time, O(m + n) space.

The two-pass structure is non-negotiable — if you wipe inline during the first pass, the zeros you write trigger more wipes and you destroy the matrix. Two passes separates *detection* from *action*."
sections.why: Two reasons to name it. (1) The two-pass structure (mark, then act) is the same structure the O(1) solution uses — we're just going to be smarter about *where* the marks live. (2) Explicitly calling out the 'inline wipe poisons the next iteration' trap shows you saw why two passes are needed before the interviewer asks. That's a free signal that you understand the algorithm, not just the recipe.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What's the trick that gets us from O(m + n) to O(1)?
sections.say:
"The insight is: I already have m + n free booleans sitting right there in the matrix — row 0 and column 0. If I want to mark row i as 'needs to be zeroed', I can write a 0 to `matrix[i][0]`. Same for columns and row 0. So I reuse the first row and first column as my flag arrays — that's the O(1) trick.

But there's a subtle conflict: row 0 and column 0 are *also* part of the matrix, so they might legitimately need to be zeroed themselves. If they originally contained a 0, that information will be overwritten the instant I start writing flags. So I need two scalar booleans — `firstRowZero` and `firstColZero` — captured BEFORE any flag-writing. Then the order becomes: (1) capture the two scalars, (2) write flags into row 0 / col 0 for the interior, (3) read flags and zero the interior, (4) finally apply the captured scalars to row 0 / col 0 themselves. Four phases, and the order is rigid — if you zero row 0 / col 0 earlier than phase 4, you destroy the flags phase 3 still needs to read."
sections.why: Naming the marker-reuse trick *and* the four-phase ordering is the move. 'Use the first row and column as flags' alone is half the answer; the rigid 'capture scalars first, apply them last' framing is what makes the answer actually work. Interviewers grade on the ordering — they'll specifically ask 'what if you applied the firstRowZero boolean right after capturing it?' to probe whether you understand the dependency.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the four-phase model before writing the loops.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover a single interior zero (canonical case), a zero in row 0 itself (the scalar boolean has to do work), and a zero in an interior position the interviewer might ask about.

examples.note: Canonical case — one interior zero at (1, 1). Row 0 and col 0 had no originals, so the scalars stay false and phase 4 is a no-op.
examples.trace:
phase 1: scan row 0 → firstRowZero=false. scan col 0 → firstColZero=false.
phase 2: scan interior. find 0 at (1, 1) → mark matrix[1][0]=0 and matrix[0][1]=0.
  matrix now: [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]]
phase 3: read flags, zero interior.
  (1, 1): matrix[1][0]=0 → write 0 (already 0). 
  (1, 2): matrix[1][0]=0 → write 0.
  (2, 1): matrix[0][1]=0 → write 0.
  matrix now: [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]]
phase 4: firstRowZero=false, firstColZero=false → no-op.
final: [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]] ✓

examples.note: Row 0 itself contains zeros. The scalars do work — firstRowZero=true, firstColZero=true (matrix[0][0]=0). Phase 4 applies them last so the flags survive phase 3.
examples.trace:
phase 1: scan row 0 → matrix[0][0]=0 and matrix[0][3]=0 → firstRowZero=true.
         scan col 0 → matrix[0][0]=0 → firstColZero=true.
phase 2: scan interior (i≥1, j≥1). no interior zeros! matrix[0] already has 0s at (0, 0) and (0, 3) — those ARE the flags for col 0 and col 3.
  matrix unchanged: [[0, 1, 2, 0], [3, 4, 5, 2], [1, 3, 1, 5]]
phase 3: read flags from row 0.
  row 1: matrix[0][1]=1, matrix[0][2]=2, matrix[0][3]=0 → zero (1, 3) only (no col 0 flag effect yet).
  row 2: same — zero (2, 3).
  matrix now: [[0, 1, 2, 0], [3, 4, 5, 0], [1, 3, 1, 0]]
phase 4: firstRowZero=true → zero entire row 0: [0, 0, 0, 0].
         firstColZero=true → zero entire col 0: matrix[i][0]=0 for all i.
final: [[0, 0, 0, 0], [0, 4, 5, 0], [0, 3, 1, 0]] ✓

examples.note: Cross through (1, 1) — interior zero, no row-0/col-0 effect. The scalars stay false, phase 4 no-op. Demonstrates the 'cross' shape cleanly.
examples.trace:
phase 1: scan row 0 → firstRowZero=false. scan col 0 → firstColZero=false.
phase 2: scan interior. find 0 at (1, 1) → matrix[1][0]=0, matrix[0][1]=0.
  matrix now: [[1, 0, 3], [0, 0, 6], [7, 8, 9]]
phase 3: read flags, zero interior.
  (1, 1): matrix[1][0]=0 → 0. (1, 2): matrix[1][0]=0 → 0.
  (2, 1): matrix[0][1]=0 → 0. (2, 2): neither flag set → unchanged.
  matrix now: [[1, 0, 3], [0, 0, 0], [7, 0, 9]]
phase 4: both scalars false → no-op.
final: [[1, 0, 3], [0, 0, 0], [7, 0, 9]] ✓

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two bugs this problem rewards. (1) Capturing the scalars too late — if you scan row 0 / col 0 *after* phase 2, you've already overwritten them with flags, and `firstRowZero` will be true whenever any interior column had a zero (because phase 2 wrote a 0 into row 0 to mark it). (2) Applying the scalars too early — if you zero row 0 right after phase 2 instead of waiting until phase 4, you wipe the flags that phase 3 still needs to read for the interior. Both bugs pass the canonical 'single interior zero' test and fail the harder 'zero in row 0' test.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Single row (1 × n) → there is no interior; the whole matrix IS row 0. The interior loops never run. The firstRowZero scalar does all the work — if the row contains any 0, the whole row gets wiped in phase 4. ✓
• Single column (m × 1) → mirror image — firstColZero does all the work.
• 1 × 1 matrix → if it's 0, firstRowZero=true and firstColZero=true → wiped (still 0, trivially). If it's nonzero, nothing happens.
• No zeros at all → both scalars stay false, phase 2 marks nothing, phase 3 zeros nothing, phase 4 no-op. Matrix unchanged. ✓
• Matrix entirely of zeros → every cell triggers, every flag gets set, everything ends up 0. ✓
• Matrix.length === 0 — guard with an early return, otherwise `matrix[0].length` throws.
• Big trap to flag explicitly: do NOT use the same scan-and-wipe loop for the interior; the order must be 'mark all, then act'. Otherwise zeros written in phase 2/3 cascade."
sections.why: The single-row and single-column edges are the ones where the algorithm collapses to just the scalars — surfacing them shows the scalars aren't decorative for the general case, they're load-bearing for the degenerate ones. The 'do not scan-and-wipe in the same loop' callout is the load-bearing constraint that distinguishes this algorithm from the naive approach the user was almost going to write — saying it out loud before the interviewer asks is the move.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(m * n) — we touch every cell a constant number of times across the four phases (scan row 0, scan col 0, scan interior twice, then write row 0 / col 0). No nested unbounded loops, so the bound is tight.

Space is O(1) extra — just the two scalar booleans `firstRowZero` and `firstColZero`. The flag 'arrays' are reusing existing matrix cells, so they don't count toward extra space.

The 'reuse part of the input as auxiliary storage' template shows up elsewhere — encode-decode strings packs length prefixes into the encoded string itself. Move zeroes uses the array's tail as the 'zero parking lot'. In-place quicksort uses a single pivot cell as the partition boundary. The general principle: when O(1) extra space is the constraint, look for k cells of the input that can be repurposed as bookkeeping, capture their original semantics in scalars first, and restore them at the end."
sections.why: The 'reuse the input as scratch space' framing is the senior-candidate framing — it generalizes this problem to a family rather than memorizing the row-0/col-0 trick. The encode-decode and move-zeroes connections prove you see the template, not just this problem. Interviewers love hearing 'this is a special case of a more general technique' because it suggests you'll pattern-match the next problem in the family without help.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the four-phase in-place zeroing. Phase 1 captures whether row 0 / col 0 originally had any zero. Phase 2 marks the interior by writing flags into row 0 / col 0. Phase 3 reads those flags and zeros the interior. Phase 4 finally applies the captured booleans to row 0 / col 0 themselves.

examples.label: 3x3 single interior zero → ring of zeros around center
3x4 row-0 has zeros → top row + first/last col wiped
3x3 interior zero at (1,1) → cross through row 1, col 1

alternates.label: Marker Sets (O(m+n) space)
alternates.when: Reach for this when interview pressure is high and the O(1) trick doesn't come to mind — two boolean arrays (one per row, one per column) make the two-pass structure obvious and are easy to reason about. The only cost is O(m+n) auxiliary space.
notes: Two explicit boolean arrays replace the implicit flags reused from row 0 / col 0 — easier to read but O(m+n) extra space.
Same two-pass structure as the optimal: detect zeros first, apply them second (avoids cascade writes).
No scalar booleans needed — the arrays are never overwritten, so row-0/col-0 ambiguity disappears.

questions.q: Why capture `firstRowZero` and `firstColZero` before scanning the interior?
options: Because the interior scan visits row 0 / col 0 cells first and could short-circuit before reaching real zeros
Because the first row and column get reused as flag storage and would otherwise lose their original zero info
Because the JS engine may reorder loop iterations and reading the scalars first guarantees a consistent snapshot
Because zeros in row 0 / col 0 trigger different row+column wipes than interior zeros do (only row, not column)

questions.q: Space complexity of the optimal in-place approach?
options: O(m + n) for two separate flag arrays
O(min(m, n)) — one flag array indexed by the smaller dimension

questions.q: Why must the first row / first column be zeroed LAST?
options: Because zeroing them first would propagate zeros via the cascade trap the two-pass design is meant to prevent
If you zero them earlier, you destroy the flags the interior pass still needs to read
Because the interior pass writes flags into row 0 / col 0 and they must be in a known state when written
So that the scalars `firstRowZero` and `firstColZero` can be re-derived from the matrix at the end for verification
O((m + n)^2) for the cross-shaped wipe per zero
